title: New 'fire amoeba' could assist scientists in finding alien life
excerpt: Previous research has shown that complex multicellular organisms could only reproduce in temperatures up to 140 degrees.
content:

Updated Thu, October 1, 2026 at 3:04 PM UTC

Previous research has shown that complex multicellular organisms could only reproduce in temperatures up to 140 degrees.

(NewsNation) — NASA-funded researchers have recently discovered a type of extremophile that defies what was previously known about the conditions complex organisms can survive and proliferate in. The amoeba could help scientists in their search for alien life.

Incendiamoeba cascadensis, nicknamed the 'fire amoeba,' was discovered by scientists in the hot waters of Lassen Volcanic National Park in California.

An extremophile is an organism that can exist in extreme environments: acidity, temperature, chemical composition, or alkaliphilic. The fire amoeba is a thermophile, an organism able to survive in extreme heat. The amoeba can reproduce through cellular division at 145 degrees Fahrenheit. The amoeba stops reproducing at higher temperatures but can survive in temperatures up to 176 degrees.

Previous research has shown that complex multicellular organisms could only reproduce in temperatures up to 140 degrees. Complex multicellular organisms, eukaryotes, are particularly vulnerable to high temperatures because they contain a nucleus and a membrane that can be broken down in extreme heat, according to a statement by NASA. Due to this fact, research of thermophiles has focused primarily on single-celled organisms or prokaryotes

“In part, studies on eukaryotes may have been limited because of assumptions about membrane stability,” Lead author of the study and graduate student at Syracuse University Beryl Rappaport said. “We are hoping that the discovery of I. cascadensis encourages others to keep searching for high-temperature eukaryotes.”

The fire amoeba could be instrumental in assisting scientists in their search for alien life, as it widens our understanding of what environments multicellular life can proliferate in.

“Studying extremophiles helps us better understand the biochemical and physiological limitations of life as we know it on Earth,” Program scientist for Exobiology at NASA Headquarters Alison Olcott said. “This information, in turn, helps guide NASA’s search for life as it expands the range of conditions we think life could potentially be inhabiting elsewhere.”

The key to understanding how the fire amoeba survives lies in its genes. Scientists have discovered that the amoeba has specific adaptations that prevent the breakdown of DNA in extreme heat. The adaptations also allow the fire amoeba to be able to sense the temperature of its environment.

Although its discovery reshapes our understanding of the conditions complex life can survive on Earth, scientists caution that the ingredients for life go beyond temperature. Earth is the only planet we know of that has the right conditions for the fire amoeba to proliferate.

“It could certainly be possible for complex life like I. Cascadensis to survive on another planet, but Earth is the only planet we currently know of to have all the requirements for I. Cascadensis to be happy,” Rappaport said. “It’s not just about temperature. An environment also needs the right acidity, oxygen levels, pressure, water, and food. I. Cascadensis could not survive on its own. It needs other life to be supported as well.”
